lessons.title: War & the Soldier's Experience
lessons.content_html:
War & the Soldier’s Experience

The Conflict poetry collection in the OCR anthology spans centuries of warfare, from the Napoleonic era to modern conflicts. This lesson focuses on poems that place the reader directly inside the experience of combat — the fear before battle, the chaos of violence, and the psychological cost of survival. These poems challenge the idea that war is glorious, instead presenting it as brutal, terrifying, and dehumanising.

The poets in this group often wrote from personal experience or in direct response to specific wars. Understanding the historical context of each conflict helps explain why the poets chose particular diction and imagery to convey the reality of warfare.

Key Fact

Soldier-experience poems in the anthology typically explore three aspects: the physical reality of combat (violence, injury, death), the psychological impact (fear, trauma, moral conflict), and the gap between expectation and reality (propaganda vs truth, glory vs horror).

The Charge of the Light Brigade — Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1854)

Tennyson wrote this poem in response to a newspaper report about a disastrous cavalry charge during the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War. Due to a miscommunicated order, about 670 British soldiers charged directly into Russian artillery. About 110 were killed and about 130 wounded. Tennyson, the Poet Laureate, wrote the poem to honour the soldiers’ bravery despite the incompetence of their commanders.

The poem’s dactylic metre (“HALF a league, HALF a league”) mimics the rhythm of galloping horses, pulling the reader into the charge. The anaphora “Cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them, / Cannon in front of them” creates a sense of being surrounded and trapped. The repeated refrain “Into the valley of Death” (an allusion to Psalm 23) transforms the battlefield into a hellish landscape.

“Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die.” This famous couplet captures the soldiers’ absolute obedience. The parallel structure (“Theirs not… / Theirs but…”) reduces their role to two actions: doing and dying. The rhyme of “why” and “die” links questioning with death — in the military, soldiers who question orders face the same fate. Tennyson presents this obedience as both noble and tragic: noble because of their courage, tragic because someone had “blundered.”

Bayonet Charge — Ted Hughes (1957)

Hughes’s poem imagines a World War I soldier mid-charge across no man’s land. Unlike Tennyson’s collective heroism, Hughes focuses on a single, unnamed soldier whose patriotic ideals collapse under the reality of combat. The poem opens in medias res (“Suddenly he awoke and was running”), plunging the reader into chaos without preparation — just as the soldier experiences it.

The central stanza presents the soldier frozen in thought: “In what cold clockwork of the stars and the nations / Was he the hand pointing that second?” The metaphor of “cold clockwork” suggests war is a vast, impersonal mechanism — the soldier is just a cog, a “hand pointing,” stripped of individual will. Hughes then delivers the devastating objective correlative: a hare “rolled like a flame” in agony, which jolts the soldier back into action — not from courage, but from animal instinct to survive.

Key Fact

Hughes uses the hare — “rolled like a flame” with a “threshing circle” of agony — as an objective correlative for the soldier’s own suffering. The hare is an innocent creature caught in mechanised violence, just like the soldier. Its appearance breaks the soldier’s paralysis, but he charges forward from animal terror, not patriotic duty — “King, honour, human dignity, etcetera / Dropped like luxuries.”

Comparing Soldier Poems

Similarity: Both poems describe soldiers charging into lethal danger. Both acknowledge the senselessness of the situation — Tennyson’s “Someone had blundered” and Hughes’s “cold clockwork of the stars” both suggest the individual soldier has no control.

Difference: Tennyson writes about a collective (“the six hundred”) and ultimately celebrates their bravery: “Honour the Light Brigade.” Hughes focuses on a single, anonymous soldier and strips away all nobility — patriotism is a “luxury” discarded under fire.

Context: Tennyson wrote as Poet Laureate with a public duty to honour the dead. Hughes wrote after two World Wars had shattered the myth of glorious combat. The century between them transforms the soldier from celebrated hero to traumatised individual.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing soldier-experience poems, focus on the attitude to conflict rather than just describing what happens. Tennyson memorialises the soldiers; Hughes dehumanises the experience. This distinction — how the poet positions the reader towards war — is the key to a top-band response. Always link the attitude to the poet’s context (AO3).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Tennyson’s “The Charge of the Light Brigade” uses dactylic metre, anaphora, and biblical allusion to honour soldiers’ obedient bravery despite a military blunder.
  • Hughes’s “Bayonet Charge” uses in medias res, the “cold clockwork” metaphor, and the hare image to strip away patriotic ideals and reveal war as animal terror.
  • Comparing across the century shows how attitudes to soldiers shifted from collective heroism to individual psychological trauma.

lessons.title: Impact of War on Others
lessons.content_html:
The Impact of War on Others

While some conflict poems focus on soldiers in battle, others explore the ripple effects of war on those who were never on the front line: the mothers who wait, the children who grow up in the shadow of conflict, and the communities destroyed by violence. These poems remind us that war’s damage extends far beyond the battlefield.

The poets in this group use different perspectives — a mother at home, a photographer processing images, a speaker addressing a distant conflict — to show that war is not just a military event but a human catastrophe that touches everyone. The shift in perspective from soldier to civilian is itself a political act: it challenges the idea that war is only the business of those who fight.

Key Fact

The “impact of war on others” poems focus on three groups: families left behind (grief, absence, waiting), witnesses who see war’s consequences (photographers, journalists, bystanders), and communities affected by displacement, destruction, and lasting trauma. These poems shift the focus from heroism to suffering.

War Photographer — Carol Ann Duffy (1985)

Duffy’s poem follows a war photographer developing his photographs in a darkroom after returning from a conflict zone. The poem contrasts the “ordered rows” of film spools with the chaos they contain, and the “Rural England” of the photographer’s home with the war zones he has witnessed. The opening simile — spools “ordered rows” are “as though this were a church and he / a priest preparing to intone a Mass” — gives the darkroom a sacred quality, as if developing photographs is a religious act of witnessing.

The poem’s most powerful moment comes when an image begins to materialise: “A stranger’s features / faintly start to twist before his eyes, / a half-formed ghost.” The ghost metaphor suggests the subject is already dead — captured only as a haunting trace. The final stanza delivers Duffy’s critique: the readers back in England see the photos but “do not care” — they feel a momentary pang before turning to the next page. The poem indicts comfortable indifference to suffering.

“The reader’s eyeballs prick / with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers.” Duffy uses the mundane domestic routine (“bath,” “pre-lunch beers”) to expose the shallow sympathy of newspaper readers. The juxtaposition of comfortable routine with war photography creates a damning contrast: other people’s suffering becomes a brief interruption in a comfortable life. “Eyeballs prick with tears” suggests the response is physical but superficial — a momentary reaction, not a genuine engagement with suffering.

The Emigrée — Carol Rumens (1993)

Rumens’s poem is spoken by someone who left their homeland as a child, probably fleeing conflict or political oppression. The speaker remembers the city with idealised, sunlit nostalgia: “There once was a country… I left it as a child” — the fairy-tale opening suggests the memory has been preserved in a childlike, golden light. Despite hearing that the city is now “sick with tyrants,” the speaker’s memory remains stubbornly positive: “My city takes me dancing through the city / of walls.”

The poem explores how conflict creates displacement that lasts a lifetime. The speaker’s language is caught between two worlds: they still carry the “original view” of their city even though that city may no longer exist. The first stanza’s image of the speaker “branded by an impression of sunlight” suggests identity is marked by the place you come from — conflict cannot erase it, even when it destroys the place itself.

Key Fact

Rumens shows conflict’s lasting impact through three ideas: the speaker’s idealised memory refuses to accept the city’s destruction, their identity remains “branded” by a homeland they can never return to, and the gap between past beauty and present violence creates a permanent emotional displacement.

Comparing Impact Poems

Similarity: Both poems explore the gap between direct experience of conflict and the distance of safety. Both speakers carry war’s images with them — the photographer through film, the emigrée through memory.

Difference: Duffy critiques those who are indifferent to suffering; Rumens explores how a victim of conflict preserves their identity. Duffy’s tone is angry and accusatory; Rumens’s is nostalgic and defiant.

Context: Both poets write about late 20th-century conflicts where media coverage brought images of war into comfortable Western homes. Duffy responds to this media saturation; Rumens responds to the refugee experience of displacement and memory.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Poems about war’s impact on others make excellent comparison choices because they shift the perspective away from soldiers. In your comparison, identify who is speaking, what they witness, and how the poet positions the reader. This perspective analysis is a strong AO2 strategy that many students overlook.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Duffy’s “War Photographer” uses the darkroom setting and religious imagery to give war photography a sacred quality, then critiques readers who feel only shallow sympathy.
  • Rumens’s “The Emigrée” explores how conflict creates permanent displacement — the speaker’s idealised memory of their homeland resists the reality of its destruction.
  • Both poems show that war’s damage extends far beyond the battlefield, affecting witnesses, refugees, and distant readers in different ways.

lessons.title: Inner Conflict & Anger
lessons.content_html:
Inner Conflict & Anger

Not all conflict in the OCR anthology takes place on a battlefield. Some of the most powerful poems explore inner conflict — the battles fought inside the mind. These poems present anger, frustration, moral dilemma, and the struggle between what we feel and what we are expected to feel. Studying them alongside war poems reveals that “conflict” is a far broader concept than military combat.

Key Fact

Inner conflict in the anthology takes three main forms: moral conflict (struggling with right and wrong), emotional conflict (anger, grief, or frustration that cannot be expressed), and identity conflict (tension between who you are and who society expects you to be). These internal battles can be as destructive as physical warfare.

A Poison Tree — William Blake (1794)

Blake’s deceptively simple poem uses the allegory of a growing tree to show how suppressed anger becomes deadly. The opening stanza establishes the contrast: “I was angry with my friend: / I told my wrath, my wrath did end. / I was angry with my foe: / I told it not, my wrath did grow.” Expressed anger dissolves; suppressed anger grows.

The tree is “watered” with fears and “sunned” with smiles — Blake inverts natural imagery to show how deceit nourishes resentment. The “apple bright” that grows is a clear allusion to the Garden of Eden: suppressed anger becomes temptation, and the foe who eats it is found “outstretched beneath the tree” — dead. The final image is chilling because the speaker seems glad: “In the morning glad I see.”

Blake personifies anger as a living thing that needs nurturing. “Watered” with tears and “sunned” with “soft deceitful wiles” uses the semantic field of gardening — but what grows is poison, not beauty. The regular AABB rhyme and simple diction give the poem a nursery-rhyme quality that makes the dark content more disturbing — like a children’s story with a murderous ending.

Half-caste — John Agard (1996)

Agard’s poem is an angry, humorous response to the offensive term “half-caste.” The speaker dismantles the word by applying its logic to art: “Explain yuself / wha yu mean / when yu say half-caste / yu mean when Picasso / mix red an green / is a half-caste canvas?” If mixing colours in painting is genius, why is mixing races considered incomplete? The phonetic spelling (“yu,” “dem,” “wha”) asserts the speaker’s Caribbean identity — refusing to adopt “proper” English is itself an act of resistance.

The poem builds through repetition of “Explain yuself” — a challenge that demands the listener justify their prejudice. The ending shifts from humour to power: “But yu must come back tomorrow / wid de whole of yu eye / an de whole of yu ear / an de whole of yu mind.” The implication is devastating — anyone who uses “half-caste” is the one who is incomplete, seeing with half an eye and thinking with half a mind.

Key Fact

Agard turns the insult back on the user: if the speaker is “half-caste,” then they can only offer “half a hand,” “half a dream,” and “half a shadow.” But the final demand for “de whole of yu mind” implies that it is the prejudiced person who is incomplete — they see the world with only half their understanding.

Comparing Inner Conflict Poems

Similarity: Both poems explore anger as a response to injustice. Both use deceptively simple language and repetitive structures to deliver serious messages.

Difference: Blake’s anger is suppressed and becomes deadly — the poem warns against hiding true feelings. Agard’s anger is openly expressed as a tool of resistance and empowerment — speaking out dismantles prejudice. Blake’s speaker is complicit in the harm; Agard’s is fighting it.

Context: Blake wrote during the Romantic period, challenging the suppression of emotion by polite society. Agard writes as a British-Caribbean poet challenging racial prejudice in 1990s Britain. Both use poetry as a weapon against social hypocrisy.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Inner conflict poems are versatile comparison choices because they link to war poems (internal vs external conflict), love poems (emotional battles), and identity poems (social vs personal self). When comparing, always identify what the conflict is, how the poet presents it (methods), and why it matters in context (AO3).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Blake’s “A Poison Tree” uses garden allegory and biblical allusion to warn that suppressed anger becomes deadly — the poem’s nursery-rhyme form makes the dark content more disturbing.
  • Agard’s “Half-caste” uses phonetic spelling, repetition, and absurd logic to dismantle racial prejudice, turning the insult “half” back on the user.
  • Inner conflict poems broaden the definition of “conflict” beyond warfare to include emotional suppression, identity struggles, and social injustice.

lessons.title: Social Conflict & Identity
lessons.content_html:
Social Conflict & Identity

The Conflict collection includes poems that explore social and political struggles: the conflict between the powerful and the powerless, between cultural identity and forced conformity, and between individual freedom and systemic oppression. These poems broaden “conflict” beyond warfare to include the daily battles of people fighting for recognition, equality, and justice.

Key Fact

Social conflict poems in the anthology explore three types: class conflict (inequality between rich and poor, powerful and powerless), racial and cultural conflict (the struggle to assert identity against prejudice), and political conflict (resistance to tyranny, oppression, or unjust authority).

London — William Blake (1794)

Blake’s “London” presents a devastating portrait of social oppression in the late 18th-century city. The speaker walks through “charter’d streets” near the “charter’d Thames” — the repetition of charter’d suggests that even the natural river has been claimed and controlled by the powerful. In every face the speaker sees “marks of weakness, marks of woe” — the anaphora of “marks” brands suffering onto the city’s people like a physical scar.

The poem builds through a catalogue of victims: the chimney sweeper’s “cry” indicts the Church (“every blackening church appalls”), the soldier’s sigh “runs in blood down palace walls,” and the “youthful Harlot’s curse” blights the “Marriage hearse.” The juxtaposition of “Marriage” and “hearse” (a funeral carriage) suggests that even love and family are corrupted by a society built on exploitation.

“In every cry of every Man, / In every Infant’s cry of fear, / In every voice, in every ban, / The mind-forg’d manacles I hear.” The metaphor “mind-forg’d manacles” is Blake’s most famous image. “Manacles” are handcuffs — but these are “mind-forg’d,” meaning the chains are mental, not physical. Blake argues that oppression is maintained not just by law and force, but by people accepting their own subjugation. The word “forg’d” carries a double meaning: both “made” (as a blacksmith forges metal) and “faked” (forged like a counterfeit document). The chains are manufactured, artificial — they could be broken.

Checking Out Me History — John Agard (1996)

Agard’s poem is a protest against the Eurocentric curriculum that taught him about Dick Whittington and Florence Nightingale but not about Toussaint L’Ouverture (who led the Haitian Revolution) or Nanny de Maroon (who resisted British slavery in Jamaica). The poem alternates between two voices: the imposed history (“Dem tell me / Dem tell me / Wha dem want to tell me”) in standard layout, and the reclaimed history in italicised, lyrical stanzas celebrating Black heroes.

The refrain “Dem tell me” exposes education as a form of control — “dem” (they) decided what history was worth knowing. The poem’s climax is defiant: “But now I checking out me own history / I carving out me identity.” The active verbs “checking out” and “carving” present the speaker taking control of their own narrative. “Carving” suggests both sculpture (creating something permanent) and effort (it requires force to carve).

Key Fact

Agard celebrates: Toussaint L’Ouverture (led the Haitian Revolution, the first successful slave revolt), Nanny de Maroon (escaped slave who led guerrilla resistance against the British in Jamaica), and Mary Seacole (Jamaican nurse who cared for soldiers in the Crimean War but was overlooked in favour of Florence Nightingale). Each represents history that the British curriculum erased.

Comparing Social Conflict Poems

Similarity: Both poets expose how powerful institutions (Church, State, education) control ordinary people. Both use repetition as a structural device to hammer home systemic oppression. Both argue that awareness is the first step to freedom.

Difference: Blake’s poem is despairing — the “mind-forg’d manacles” suggest people are trapped by their own acceptance. Agard’s is empowering — “I carving out me identity” shows the speaker breaking free. Blake observes oppression; Agard actively resists it.

Context: Blake wrote during the Industrial Revolution when workers had almost no rights. Agard writes as a post-colonial poet whose education was shaped by the British Empire. Both challenge the systems that keep people ignorant of their own oppression.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Social conflict poems work brilliantly alongside war poems for comparison — both explore power, oppression, and resistance. When comparing, focus on who holds power, how it is maintained, and whether the poem ends with hope or despair. This “power dynamic” analysis impresses examiners because it shows you understand the poems’ political messages (AO1 + AO3).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Blake’s “London” uses “charter’d,” “mind-forg’d manacles,” and the “Marriage hearse” to present a city where every institution — Church, State, family — perpetuates suffering.
  • Agard’s “Checking Out Me History” uses dual voices, phonetic spelling, and active verbs to reclaim erased Black history and assert identity against a Eurocentric curriculum.
  • Both poems expose systemic control, but Blake is despairing while Agard is defiantly empowered.

lessons.title: Form, Structure & Language
lessons.content_html:
Form, Structure & Language in Conflict Poetry

AO2 requires you to analyse how poets present conflict, not just what they say about it. The Conflict collection uses an extraordinary range of methods: metre that mimics galloping horses or marching feet, sound devices that recreate the noise of battle, and structural choices that mirror chaos or rigid military order.

Key Fact

AO2 assesses: Form (e.g. Tennyson’s dactylic metre mimicking cavalry), Structure (e.g. Hughes’s in medias res plunging the reader into action, Agard’s dual-voice layout), and Language (e.g. Blake’s “mind-forg’d manacles” metaphor, Duffy’s religious simile for the darkroom).

Form: Shape & Sound

Form in conflict poetry often enacts its subject. Tennyson’s dactylic metre (DAH-duh-duh) in “The Charge of the Light Brigade” sounds like galloping hooves. By contrast, Hughes’s “Bayonet Charge” uses enjambment and irregular line lengths to create the breathless, stumbling movement of a soldier running across no man’s land.

Blake’s “A Poison Tree” uses AABB couplets and simple diction to create a nursery-rhyme quality. This innocent form makes the murderous content more disturbing. Agard’s “Half-caste” deliberately avoids standard punctuation and uses phonetic spelling, making the form itself an act of resistance against English literary conventions.

In medias res (Hughes): Starting in the middle of action creates immediate disorientation — no context, no preparation, just chaos.

Dual-voice layout (Agard): Alternating between imposed and reclaimed history creates a visual and thematic contrast on the page itself.

Refrain (Tennyson): Repeated “valley of Death” and “the six hundred” create a memorial, ritual quality.

Volta (Duffy): The shift in “War Photographer” from the darkroom’s solemnity to the readers’ indifference creates a damning structural contrast.

Language: Imagery, Sound & Diction

Conflict poets use onomatopoeia, harsh consonants, and violent imagery to recreate the sensory experience of conflict. Hughes’s “bullets smacking the belly out of the air” uses the plosive “b” sounds and violent verb “smacking” to make the reader hear gunfire. Blake’s “blood down palace walls” uses visceral imagery to link the State directly to soldiers’ deaths.

Diction — the level of language — also conveys meaning. Compare Tennyson’s elevated, formal register (“Honour the charge they made!”) with Agard’s deliberately informal, oral register (“Explain yuself”). The formality reflects Tennyson’s role as Poet Laureate; Agard’s informality is a rejection of the literary establishment.

Key Fact

The strongest AO2 analysis connects sound to meaning: plosive consonants recreate violence, sibilance suggests stealth or suffering, dactylic metre mimics movement. Never just name a device — explain what it makes the reader experience and why the poet chose it.

Charge of the Light Brigade: Dactylic metre, anaphora, refrain, biblical allusion, imperative.

Bayonet Charge: In medias res, enjambment, objective correlative (hare), metaphor, plosive alliteration.

War Photographer: Religious simile, juxtaposition, ghost metaphor, accusatory tone, volta.

London: Anaphora, metaphor (“mind-forg’d manacles”), oxymoron (“Marriage hearse”), ABAB rhyme.

A Poison Tree: Allegory, biblical allusion, AABB couplets, semantic field of gardening.

Half-caste / Checking Out Me History: Phonetic spelling, repetitive refrain, dual voices, active verbs.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Never write “The poet uses alliteration to make the poem interesting.” Instead, specify which sounds, quote them, and explain the effect: “Hughes’s plosive alliteration in ‘bullets smacking the belly’ forces the reader to hear the percussive violence of gunfire, making the experience visceral rather than abstract.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Form in conflict poetry often enacts its subject: dactylic metre for cavalry, enjambment for chaos, couplets for deceptive simplicity.
  • Structural features (in medias res, dual voices, refrain, volta) control the reader’s experience and should be analysed as deliberate choices.
  • Language analysis must connect sound to meaning — explain what the reader hears, sees, or feels, not just name the device.

lessons.title: Comparing Across Time
lessons.content_html:
Comparing Across Time Periods

The Conflict collection spans from Blake’s Romantic-era protest (1794) through Victorian war poetry (Tennyson, 1854) to contemporary responses (Duffy, Agard, Hughes). Comparing poems from different eras is essential for AO3 because it shows you understand why attitudes to conflict change over time. The key shift is from conflict as something honourable and necessary to conflict as something brutal, unjust, and psychologically devastating.

Key Fact

The key shift is from conflict as duty and honour (Tennyson’s memorial to brave soldiers) to conflict as trauma and injustice (Hughes’s individual terror, Duffy’s critique of indifference). The two World Wars shattered the myth of glorious combat. Post-colonial poets like Agard expanded “conflict” to include cultural and racial struggles.

Three Eras of Conflict Poetry

Romantic Era (Blake, 1794): Blake challenged the establishment through protest poetry. “London” attacks institutional corruption. Conflict here is social and political — the powerful against the powerless. Blake’s radical politics anticipated later movements for workers’ rights and democracy.

Victorian Era (Tennyson, 1854): Tennyson wrote as Poet Laureate — an official voice. His duty was to honour the soldiers, even while acknowledging the military “blunder” that caused their deaths. The poem reflects a society that valued obedience, duty, and sacrifice. Criticising the war itself would have been almost unthinkable.

Modern Era (Hughes, Duffy, Agard, Rumens): After two World Wars, Vietnam, and the Troubles, poets had no illusions about war’s glory. Hughes strips away patriotism to reveal animal terror. Duffy exposes comfortable indifference. Agard and Rumens expand “conflict” to include racial, cultural, and identity struggles. The modern poets question rather than memorialise.

Tennyson’s soldiers are a collective (“the six hundred”) defined by obedience: “Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die.” The parallel structure reduces them to a single function, but the imperative “Honour the Light Brigade” elevates that function to something sacred. Tennyson writes within a Victorian culture that valued duty above individual feeling.

Hughes’s soldier is a nameless individual whose patriotic ideals — “King, honour, human dignity, etcetera” — are “dropped like luxuries” under fire. The dismissive “etcetera” is devastating: it reduces Tennyson’s sacred values to an afterthought. Hughes writes after 1945, when the myth of glorious sacrifice had been permanently destroyed by industrialised warfare.

Context link: The century between them transforms the soldier from celebrated hero to traumatised individual. This shift reflects a society that has witnessed the mechanised slaughter of two World Wars and can no longer accept the idea that dying for your country is automatically noble.

Embedding Context in Conflict Comparisons

When comparing conflict poems across time, use context to explain why the poets differ. Do not just list historical facts — connect them to specific textual evidence. Three effective strategies:

1. Explain method through context: “Tennyson’s dactylic metre honours the soldiers through rhythm, reflecting his Laureate’s duty to memorialise; Hughes’s enjambment recreates chaos, reflecting a post-war distrust of orderly narratives about conflict.”

2. Explain attitude through context: “Blake’s anger at ‘charter’d streets’ reflects Romantic radicalism — a belief that institutions corrupt natural human freedom. Agard’s anger at ‘Dem tell me’ reflects post-colonial awareness — a recognition that education itself was a tool of Empire.”

3. Explain genre through context: “Tennyson writes a memorial poem because his society expected poets to commemorate sacrifice. Duffy writes an accusatory poem because her society has the luxury of distant observation, not direct participation.”

Key Fact

Context in conflict poetry is most effective when it explains a shift in attitude: from duty to trauma, from honour to disillusionment, from national pride to individual suffering. Always link this shift to specific historical events (World Wars, post-colonial independence) and their effect on how poets understood conflict.

Avoid: “In the Victorian era, life was hard” (too vague). “Tennyson was born in 1809” (biography, not context). “All war poets hated war” (not true — Tennyson honours it). “Hughes fought in World War I” (he did not — he imagines a WWI soldier). Always check your facts and make context specific to the poem.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The strongest contextual comparisons explain a shift: “While Tennyson, writing in 1854, could still present military obedience as noble, Hughes, writing after two World Wars, reduces patriotic values to ‘luxuries’ discarded under fire. This shift reflects a century of disillusionment with the myth of glorious sacrifice.” This kind of comparative context earns both AO1 and AO3 marks simultaneously.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Conflict collection spans Romantic, Victorian, and Modern eras — each brings different attitudes shaped by different historical experiences of conflict.
  • The key shift is from conflict as duty/honour (Tennyson) to conflict as trauma/injustice (Hughes, Duffy), expanded by post-colonial poets to include cultural and racial conflict (Agard, Rumens).

lessons.title: Comparison Skills
lessons.content_html:
Comparison Skills for Conflict Poetry

The OCR poetry question comes in two parts, each worth 20 marks. Part (a) names one anthology poem and asks you to compare it with an unseen poem printed on the paper. Part (b) asks a related question on a different anthology poem that you choose. For the Conflict collection, you need a poem that shares a theme but differs in attitude, method, or era. This lesson teaches the practical skills of building a sustained comparison across 4–5 paragraphs, hitting AO1 (response), AO2 (methods), and AO3 (context) in each.

Key Fact

Every comparison paragraph needs: 1) A topic sentence stating the comparison point, 2) Analysis of Poem A with quotation and method, 3) A comparative connective, 4) Analysis of Poem B with quotation and method, 5) An embedded context link explaining why the poets differ.

Choosing Your Comparison Poem

Strong conflict comparisons involve poems that share a subject but take different positions. If the named poem is about soldiers, choose another soldier poem for close comparison or a civilian-impact poem for contrast. If it is about social conflict, choose another social poem or a war poem to show how “conflict” has multiple meanings.

Soldiers across time: Charge of the Light Brigade + Bayonet Charge — collective honour vs individual terror.

Impact on others: War Photographer + The Emigrée — witnessing vs remembering.

Social vs military: London + Bayonet Charge — systemic oppression vs physical warfare.

Anger and resistance: A Poison Tree + Half-caste — suppressed vs expressed anger.

Model Comparison Paragraph

Here is a model paragraph using the five-step structure:

“Both Tennyson and Hughes present soldiers mid-charge, but their attitudes to duty differ sharply. Tennyson’s soldiers embody collective obedience — ‘Theirs but to do and die’ reduces their role to two actions, presenting sacrifice as noble. In contrast, Hughes’s soldier abandons patriotic ideals: ‘King, honour, human dignity, etcetera / Dropped like luxuries.’ The dismissive ‘etcetera’ reduces Tennyson’s sacred values to an afterthought. This shift reflects a century of disillusionment — after two World Wars, glorious sacrifice could no longer be sustained.”

Notice: topic sentence (both present soldiers, but differ), Poem A analysis with quotation, comparative connective (“In contrast”), Poem B analysis with quotation, and context explaining the shift.

Key Fact

Use varied connectives: similarities (“Similarly,” “Both poets suggest”), differences (“However,” “In contrast,” “Whereas”), nuance (“While both explore…, they differ in”). Avoid using the same connective twice.

Two separate analyses: Writing about Poem A for three paragraphs, then Poem B for three, is NOT comparison. Discuss both poems in every paragraph.

Only similarities: The best comparisons explore both similarities AND differences.

Describing not analysing: Retelling events is not comparison. Focus on how poets present ideas (AO2) and why (AO3).
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the conflict comparison, examiners look for sustained comparison throughout. Never let more than two sentences pass without referencing the other poem. If you find yourself writing only about one poem, stop and add a comparative link.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Choose a comparison poem that shares a theme but differs in attitude, method, or era.
  • Every paragraph must contain analysis of both poems, linked by comparative connectives, with embedded context.
  • Avoid writing two separate analyses, finding only similarities, or describing without analysing.

lessons.title: Exam Technique & Quotation Bank
lessons.content_html:
Exam Technique: The Conflict Comparison

The poetry question is compulsory and comes in two parts, each worth 20 marks. Part (a) names one anthology poem and asks you to compare it with an unseen poem printed on the paper. Part (b) asks a related question on a different anthology poem that you choose. Balance AO1 (response), AO2 (methods), and AO3 (context) across 4–5 paragraphs. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for exact mark weightings and timings.

Key Fact

Split your time roughly: a short planning stage (choose poem, identify 3–4 points, select quotations), the main writing stage (4–5 paragraphs), and a final checking stage (add any missing AO2 terminology or AO3 context). The plan saves time by preventing mid-essay confusion about what to write next.

The Quick Plan

Step 1: Identify the theme. Underline the key word in the question.

Step 2: Choose your comparison poem. Write it down immediately.

Step 3: Note 3–4 comparison points with a quotation from each poem and the method you will analyse.

Q: Compare how the reality of conflict is presented in ‘Bayonet Charge’ and one other poem.

Choice: The Charge of the Light Brigade — both about soldiers charging, different eras.

Point 1: Opening — Hughes: in medias res, chaos. Tennyson: dactylic metre, momentum. Context: post-war vs Victorian honour.

Point 2: Attitude to duty — Hughes: “luxuries” dropped. Tennyson: “do and die.” Shift in values.

Point 3: Imagery — Hughes: hare as objective correlative. Tennyson: “valley of Death” (biblical). Different emotional registers.

Point 4: Form — Hughes: enjambment = chaos. Tennyson: regular stanzas = memorial. AO2 focus.

Quotation Bank: Conflict Collection

Memorise 2–3 short quotations per poem. Short quotes (3–5 words) are easier to remember and more effective when embedded in your sentence.

Charge of the Light Brigade: “valley of Death” | “do and die” | “Someone had blundered” | “Cannon to right of them”

Bayonet Charge: “cold clockwork of the stars” | “Dropped like luxuries” | “rolled like a flame” | “bullets smacking the belly”

War Photographer: “ordered rows” | “half-formed ghost” | “between the bath and pre-lunch beers” | “do not care”

The Emigrée: “My city takes me dancing through the city / of walls” | “branded by an impression of sunlight” | “sick with tyrants” | “original view”

London: “charter’d streets” | “mind-forg’d manacles” | “blood down palace walls” | “Marriage hearse”

A Poison Tree: “I told my wrath, my wrath did end” | “watered it in fears” | “apple bright” | “glad I see”

Half-caste: “Explain yuself” | “half-caste canvas” | “de whole of yu mind”

Checking Out Me History: “Dem tell me” | “I carving out me identity” | “Toussaint”

Key Fact

Embed quotations within your sentence: “Hughes presents patriotic values as ‘luxuries’ discarded under fire” is stronger than “Hughes writes: ‘King, honour, human dignity, etcetera / Dropped like luxuries.’” The first keeps your analysis flowing; the second interrupts it with a block quote.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the last few minutes, re-read and check: Did I compare in every paragraph? Use quotations from both poems? Name methods? Embed context at least 3 times? If anything is missing, add a sentence. These additions can push you up a mark band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Spend 5 minutes planning: choose poem, 3–4 comparison points, quotations. Stick to your plan.
  • Write 4–5 paragraphs using alternating comparison, hitting AO1, AO2, and AO3 in each.
  • Memorise 2–3 short quotations per poem and embed them in your sentences.
